newsitem.title: USA: Ohio stadium sales tax, school bonds on Tue ballot.
newsitem.headline: Ohio stadium sales tax, school bonds on Tue ballot.

text.p: Franklin County, Ohio, residents will go to the polls Tuesday to consider adding 0.5 percent to their sales tax to help finance a new soccer stadium and a hockey arena to draw the National Hockey League to downtown Columbus.
Residents of 44 school districts across Ohio will also be asked to approve bond issuances ranging from $820,000 to nearly $50.68 million.

The three-year sales tax hike for Franklin County would generate about $203 million for construction of the two facilities, according to William Jennison, executive director of the Franklin County Convention Facilities Authority.
The sales tax would take effect July 1 and revenues would fund short-term construction bonds that would be retired by the end of the three-year taxing cycle, Jennison said.

Ohio state officials would provide another $41.2 million to the project and the private sector $57.5 million for primary and secondary naming rights for the facilities, to be owned by the authority and managed by a private company, Jennison said.
Columbus is one of six finalists for a franchise in the next round of NHL expansion. The league has not set a timetable for expansion or decided how many franchises, if any, to award.
The preliminary plans for an 18,500 seat arena with 80 luxury suites and club-seating has the NHL in mind, but the arena would be feasible even without the top league, Jennison said.
"We feel pretty good about our chances (of drawing an NHL team)," Jennison said.
Columbus has a minor league hockey franchise that could draw more than 10,000 fans per game to a new downtown arena, Jennison said.

The stadium's primary tenant would be the Columbus Crew of Major League Soccer, which has averaged more than 18,000 fans per game this season, Jennison said. The stadium would have a seating capacity of 30,000 to 35,000, he added.

Jennison said the sales tax seemed the most attractive option for financing the facilities after a study found that non-residents provided about 36 percent of the total sales tax revenues collected in Franklin County.
If voters approve the tax, plans call for a groundbreaking in about one year and opening of the stadium in Spring 2000 and the arena the following fall, Jennison said.
